initial review of the three focus-group transcripts was both interesting and somewhat unsettling from an analytical perspective. The participants’ exchanges sounded natural, but the discussions did not follow a predictable sequence. Comments often shifted among browsing habits, prior purchases, website features, and reactions to visualization technology. I initially questioned how I would organize such an extensive conversational record without losing the context surrounding individual responses. I also recognized a tendency to give immediate attention to the most detailed or strongly expressed comments. That reaction reinforced the importance of becoming thoroughly familiar with the complete data set before deciding which responses are analytically significant (Braun & Clarke, 2006).

I would begin by reading each transcript independently and writing brief notes about my immediate reactions, questions, and possible assumptions. Keeping those reflections separate from the participant data would help me recognize where my interpretation might be influenced by personal expectations. I would then reread the transcripts to examine recurring language and experiences, while remaining attentive to comments that differ from the general direction of each discussion. Only after completing that process would I compare the three focus groups and begin making decisions about how the data should be organized.

The content also reminded me that participants can discuss the same experience without assigning it the same meaning. Several comments appeared to gain clarity as participants responded to one another, whereas other reactions remained individual or conditional.

While planning the data collection procedures for my proposed study, “To what extent does leadership trust predict employee knowledge-sharing behavior among middle managers in U.S. workplace organizations?”, I am focusing on maintaining alignment among the research question, variables, instruments, sampling strategy, recruitment procedures, and planned statistical analysis. Because this study uses a quantitative correlational predictive design, each data-collection step must produce the type of numerical data needed to test the relationship between leadership trust and employee knowledge-sharing behavior.

Proposed Data & Collection Steps

My proposed data-collection process will occur in the following sequence:

    Obtain the necessary approval before recruitment.
    I will complete the required Capella University Institutional Review Board (IRB) process before collecting data. The recruitment materials, informed-consent language, eligibility criteria, survey instruments, and data-collection procedures will be finalized as part of this process.
    Finalize the survey instrument.
    The survey will be administered through Qualtrics. The instrument will include informed consent, screening questions, demographic questions needed to describe the sample, the leadership trust measure, and the knowledge-sharing behavior measure. I plan to use the McAllister (1995) trust measure for leadership trust and the Van den Hooff and de Ridder (2004) knowledge-sharing measure for knowledge-sharing behavior.
    Conduct a power analysis.
    Before recruitment, I will use an a priori power analysis to determine the minimum sample size necessary for the planned simple linear regression. My current target is approximately 150–250 participants, but the final minimum will be supported by the power analysis rather than selected arbitrarily.
    Establish participant eligibility.
    Participants will be adults who work in U.S.-based workplace organizations and currently hold a middle-management or supervisory position. Participants will also need sufficient experience with their current supervisor to meaningfully evaluate leadership trust. My proposed eligibility requirement is at least six months working under the current supervisor.
    Recruit participants.
    I plan to use purposive and snowball sampling. Recruitment may occur through professional organizations, LinkedIn, relevant professional networks, and other appropriate organizational or professional channels. Recruitment materials will explain the study, eligibility requirements, voluntary nature of participation, confidentiality, and survey access.
    Administer the anonymous survey.
    Eligible participants will access the Qualtrics survey, review informed consent, complete the screening questions, and then complete the research measures. I will avoid collecting unnecessary identifying information.
    Monitor data collection.
    I will monitor response rates and eligibility while avoiding changes to the procedures that could introduce bias. I will determine whether additional recruitment is necessary based on the power analysis and the number of usable responses obtained.
    Prepare the dataset for analysis.
    After data collection closes, I will examine the dataset for incomplete responses, duplicate responses, missing data, and other data-quality concerns. I will score the instruments according to their established procedures and create composite scores for leadership trust and knowledge-sharing behavior.
    Conduct the planned statistical analysis.
    The final dataset will be analyzed using descriptive statistics and simple linear regression. The regression will test whether leadership trust statistically predicts employee knowledge-sharing behavior.

Weak or Potentially Problematic Steps

The recruitment and sampling process is currently the weakest part of my plan. Purposive and snowball sampling are appropriate for reaching a specific population that may be difficult to identify through a sampling frame, but they limit generalizability. Participants who respond through professional networks or LinkedIn may differ from eligible middle managers who do not participate in those networks.

A second concern is obtaining enough participants who meet the middle-manager eligibility criteria. Simply recruiting working adults would not adequately address the research question. I therefore need to ensure that screening questions clearly establish participants' managerial responsibilities and their experience with their current supervisor.

A third concern involves common-method bias. Participants will provide self-reported perceptions of leadership trust and their own knowledge-sharing behavior in the same survey. This creates the possibility that relationships between the variables could be influenced by the method used to collect the data rather than by the constructs themselves. Anonymous participation, clear instructions, neutral wording, and established instruments should help reduce some of this concern, although they cannot eliminate it completely.

A fourth concern is the possibility of insufficient statistical power. Recruiting a convenient number of participants is not enough. I need to complete the a priori power analysis before recruitment so that the minimum sample size is justified statistically.

Finally, instrument permissions and exact scoring procedures require additional attention. Before launching the survey, I need to verify the appropriate use or permission requirements for the selected instruments and confirm that the wording, response scale, scoring, and administration procedures are consistent with the original sources.

Support Needed to Address These Concerns

The most important support I need is guidance from my instructor and Capella's IRB resources regarding recruitment procedures, informed consent, and the appropriate use of LinkedIn and professional organizations for participant recruitment. I also need to verify whether permission is required for the selected instruments and whether the instruments can be reproduced directly in Qualtrics.

I will also use G*Power or an equivalent power-analysis resource to establish the minimum sample size for simple linear regression. This will provide a stronger justification for the planned sample than simply stating that I intend to collect 150–250 responses.

Finally, reviewing the Project Plan Alignment Tracking and Alignment Map: GuidingQuestions resources is helpful because they encourage me to examine whether every proposed data-collection step contributes directly to answering the research question rather than collecting information simply because it is available.

Data Collection & Research Gap

The alignment process is particularly important for my study because the identified gap is specific. The literature does not simply lack research on leadership, trust, or knowledge sharing. Instead, the gap concerns the specific relationship between leadership trust and employee knowledge-sharing behavior among middle managers in U.S. workplace organizations.

My alignment can be represented as:

This alignment helps prevent unnecessary data collection. For example, I do not need to collect extensive information about organizational performance, employee satisfaction, or multiple leadership styles because those variables are not necessary to answer my research question.

Thanks,

That is something I am also going to need to address in my own quantitative study because the number of participants should be statistically justified rather than based on an arbitrary target. Your concern about common method bias also stood out to me because both of your variables are being measured through the same self reported survey. I think recognizing that limitation now gives you an opportunity to build safeguards into the study before data collection begins. I am curious about your recruitment strategy, though. Since purposive and snowball sampling limit generalizability, have you considered whether a third party participant provider could identify qualified middle managers and allow you to use a probability based sampling approach instead?

The primary data-collection instrument for this Generic Qualitative Interviews study is a semi-structured, critical-incident interview protocol administered by the researcher, who is the instrument (Merriam & Tisdell, 2016; Seidman, 2019). Interviews last approximately 60–75 minutes by encrypted video conference only after informed consent and recording permission, which is the first ethical control before any infrastructure event is discussed. The protocol opens with the participant’s IT or network role and the IT disaster recovery platform-as-a-service (ITDRPaaS) or functionally equivalent external recovery platform in use, then asks for one disruption, failover, recovery test, or production recovery so that talk is anchored in a concrete infrastructure event rather than in abstract policy (Flanagan, 1954; Kvale & Brinkmann, 2015). Open-ended probes, not yes-or-no items, elicit how managers experienced who counted, who decided failover or restore, and what counted as proof that infrastructure was recoverable. Field notes captured during and immediately after each session record hesitations and reflexivity cues without scoring recovery performance or inspecting live systems. The interview guide will receive chair or methodologist expert review before Institutional Review Board submission so that wording, burden, and leading-question risk are examined before any human-subjects contact.

The methodological approach for this study will be a generic qualitative inquiry, selected to investigate how U.S. small and medium-sized enterprise (SME) IT/network managers perceive and interpret the governance challenges associated with establishing and managing IT Disaster Recovery Plan as a Service (ITDRPaaS). This approach is aligned with the study’s topic and problem, as the research aims to describe and interpret participant perceptions of governance practices as managers translate organizational IT strategy into operational disaster recovery actions. Generic qualitative inquiry is particularly suitable for this study because it focuses on understanding how individuals make sense of processes, decisions, and organizational conditions without requiring strict philosophical assumptions associated with phenomenology or other qualitative traditions (Creswell & Poth, 2016).

The general problem is that many U.S. small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) suffer avoidable organizational harm during cyber disruptions because they fail to consistently translate IT Disaster Recovery as a Service (ITDRPaaS) capabilities into governed, auditable, and defensible recover-ability assurance. This inconsistency is particularly pronounced when decision authority is fragmented and oversight is applied inconsistently under pressure (Lowry et al., 2025).

My view on IT and network managers within U.S. SMEs, who bear the responsibility for recovery while attempting to coordinate across both internal teams and external service providers in environments where stakeholder priorities are often in flux. Furthermore, existing governance frameworks frequently fail to establish clear decision rights, accountability structures, or time-sensitive escalation pathways (Erdiaw-Kwasie et al., 2017 & Mitchell et al., 1997). This responsibility of stakeholders-salience to be fascinating to see how stakeholders clamor when things go wrong withing Small and mediun IT enterprises.

The primary data source for my study will be Generic Qualitative Interviews (Changed from Lived Perspective and Initial week 2 paper), specifically semi-structured interviews, with approximately 12–15 specific selected IT Network managers/CIO/CFO from U.S. small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). These participants will have experience in implementing or overseeing IT Disaster Recovery Planning as a Service (ITDRPaaS). Purposive criterion sampling is suitable for this qualitative inquiry since it seeks information-rich participants who possess direct knowledge of the subject matter, rather than aiming for statistically representative samples (Patton, 2015). Within the Generic Qualitative Interviews framework, participants will be chosen for their ability to provide detailed insights into organizational governance processes, stakeholder interactions, decision-making authority, escalation pathways, and practices related to recoverability assurance (Merriam & Tisdell, 2016). The interviews will include a critical-incident component, allowing managers to recount specific experiences related to disruptions, fail-overs, testing, or recovery events. My interview will also explain how stakeholder pressure influenced governance actions under time constraints (Kvale & Brinkmann, 2015).

This approach directly aligns with the research purpose by enabling participants to articulate how governance decisions are understood and enacted within their organizations, rather than focusing on predetermined variables. Consequently, this primary data source will provide descriptive insights into how IT Network managers/CIO/CFO perceive stakeholder salience and its translation into decision-making authority, escalation processes, and evidence of recoverability during stakeholder ITDRPaaS-mediated recovery.

References:

Merriam, S. B., & Tisdell, E. J. (2016). Qualitative research: A guide to design and implementation (4th ed.). Jossey-Bass.

n this study, ITDRPaaS stakeholders are defined as individuals with a vested interest in the organizational, technical, governance, risk, compliance, or service-provider aspects of how U.S. small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) prepare for, govern, execute, and validate cloud-based disaster recovery. From a stakeholder-salience perspective, their importance lies in the varying degrees of influence they possess, characterized by power, legitimacy, and urgency. These factors can impact recovery priorities, decision-making authority, escalation timing, and the standards of evidence required for demonstrating recoverability (Mitchell et al., 1997). The participant pool is expected to can include IT network managers, infrastructure or cloud managers, cybersecurity and compliance managers, CFOs, CIOs, owners or senior executives with recovery decision authority, and representatives/providers who directly assist U.S. SMEs. Criterion-based purposive sampling is deemed suitable, as the goal is not to gather a statistically representative sample of all U.S. SME leadership grouping, but rather to identify approximately 10–15 information-rich participants capable of detailing the governance processes, recovery decisions, escalation events, provider dependencies, and evidence-acceptance practices related to ITDRPaaS (Merriam & Tisdell, 2016; Patton, 2015).

References:

Merriam, S. B., & Tisdell, E. J. (2016). Qualitative research: A guide to design and implementation (4th ed.). Jossey-Bass.

Mitchell, R. K., Agle, B. R., & Wood, D. J. (1997). Toward a theory of stakeholder identification and salience: Defining the principle of who and what really counts. Academy of Management Review, 22(4), 853–886.
